Population-scope guard: the national-registry figures (Levy 2025) pool EPP with X-linked protoporphyria (8.7% of the cohort); the EPP-specific share is not separately stratified for every outcome and is recorded as a guard on the edges.
governanceNotes: D1 batch 31 (2026-09-23): two bounded associations authored - an EPP-to-cholelithiasis association anchored on the early-age pigment-gallstone literature (Minder 1993 review: gallstone development at an early age is a recognized complication; Lock 1996 documents symptomatic gallstones over 20 years in a protoporphyric patient with porphyrin-rich stones) and an EPP-to-chronic-liver-disease association anchored on the Levy 2025 national longitudinal registry (322 patients: 56.2% with any liver-chemistry abnormality, 3.4% with advanced protoporphyric hepatopathy mostly requiring transplant, 62.5% of deaths attributable to liver disease) and the Meerman 2000 hepatic overview documenting protoporphyrin deposition as the hepatotoxic mechanism.

The cholelithiasis and chronic-liver-disease targets carry zero incoming edges, so no duplicate-scope conflict arises; no anemia or scarring edge is authored because EPP is not an anemia-producing porphyria (iron studies are typically normal or elevated) and cutaneous scarring lacks a catalog-fit quantified outcome - recorded as evidence gaps.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Gallstone development at an early age is a recognized EPP complication (Minder 1993 review of the disease course), porphyrin-rich pigment stones are documented in EPP patients including the Lock 1996 case with more than 20 years of symptomatic gallstones, and the mechanism literature attributes stones to excess protoporphyrin excreted in bile precipitating as pigment calculi; the overview literature records cholelithiasis as a characteristic childhood-or-early-adulthood feature of the disease.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: EPP-population gallstone prevalence is not precisely stratified in the registry literature, pigment stones share risk factors with other cholestatic and hemolytic states, and ultrasound documentation of stones with composition assessment is required rather than symptom attribution.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized protoporphyrin-pigment-stone pathway: free protoporphyrin from the heme-biosynthesis defect is excreted in bile, where its poor solubility promotes precipitation with bilirubin and calcium as dark pigment calculi; stones can form from childhood onward and may complicate the biliary tree (choledocholithiasis), compounding the protoporphyrin-induced cholestasis of severe hepatic involvement. Individual attribution requires imaging documentation of stones.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The gallstone association is mechanistically specific and review-documented but lacks precise EPP-population prevalence denominators in the cited literature; stones must be documented by imaging, composition where available, and competing stone risk factors (hemolysis, obesity, biliary disease) excluded; no probability estimate is asserted.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documented EPP (plasma or erythrocyte protoporphyrin elevation, genetic confirmation); imaging-documented cholelithiasis with chronology compatible with the disease course; stone composition where available; exclusion of hemolytic anemia, obesity, and independent biliary disease; gastroenterology assessment of the individual relationship
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Hemolytic anemia as the pigment-stone driver
Obesity, rapid weight loss, or dietary stone risk

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: the early-age pigment-gallstone association is characteristic of the disease and mechanistically specific, but population denominators are imprecise and imaging documentation is required; no causation is forced.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: In the Levy 2025 national longitudinal registry of 322 EPP/XLP patients, 56.2% had liver-chemistry abnormalities (associated with higher erythrocyte protoporphyrin levels), 3.4% had advanced protoporphyric hepatopathy with most requiring transplantation, and 62.5% of cohort deaths were attributable to liver disease; the Meerman 2000 overview documents intrahepatic protoporphyrin deposition with canalicular obstruction and progressive fibrosis as the hepatotoxic mechanism.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the registry pools EPP with X-linked protoporphyria, most chemistry abnormalities remain mild without progressive disease, and advanced hepatopathy is uncommon; individual claims require documented hepatic involvement with protoporphyrin physiology confirmed and other liver diseases excluded.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized protoporphyrin-cholestasis fibrosis pathway: excess free protoporphyrin is taken up by the liver and precipitates in canaliculi and hepatocytes, producing cholestatic injury; in a small minority the obstruction, inflammation, and repeated protoporphyrin deposition drive progressive periportal fibrosis and cirrhosis with liver failure that is transplant-dependent. The pathway is the accepted biology of protoporphyric hepatopathy; individual claims require biopsy or imaging confirmation.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Liver-chemistry abnormalities are common but advanced hepatopathy is uncommon (3.4%) and the registry pools EPP with XLP; chronic liver disease must be documented by persistent chemistry changes with imaging or histology, viral, alcoholic, and metabolic liver diseases excluded, and the transplant-requiring minority not generalized to all EPP patients; no probability estimate is asserted.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documented EPP with persistent liver-chemistry abnormalities; imaging or histologic documentation of hepatic involvement (fibrosis, protoporphyrin deposits); exclusion of viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease, and metabolic causes; hepatology assessment of the individual relationship; surveillance chronology
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, or other metabolic liver disease

evidenceGaps: Documented EPP with persistent liver-chemistry abnormalities; imaging or histologic documentation of hepatic involvement (fibrosis, protoporphyrin deposits); exclusion of viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease, and metabolic causes; hepatology assessment of the individual relationship; surveillance chronology
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: protoporphyric hepatopathy is a recognized severe complication documented in the national registry, but it affects a small minority, most chemistry changes remain mild, and the registry pools EPP with XLP; no causation or population-level severity claim is forced.
